I recommend staying on WebGLRenderer r186 for the next milestone and running a short, flag-gated WebGPURenderer test build rather than migrating now. No published millisecond costs for any three.js effect on an M1 exist, so the performance budgets in the notes are my estimates and need measuring on the MacBook. The full notes are saved to `/home/user/game-gang/research_notes/Forza level browser racing game/rendering_platform_performance.md`.

**Why not switch now:**
- **Split-screen is buggy on WebGPU.** A June 2026 forum report (r184) says the new post-processing pipeline ignores per-viewport `setViewport`/`setScissor`. Issue #34671 (render-target viewport and scissor ignored) is closed for r187. Negative scissor values are rejected (#30450).
- **It costs more CPU per draw call.** A May 2026 r183 benchmark measured 4.5 ms per frame on WebGLRenderer against 9.7 ms on WebGPURenderer. The cold first frame was 32 ms against 167 ms, and 344 ms with WebGPURenderer forced onto its WebGL backend.
- **The port is real work.** `ShaderMaterial`, `onBeforeCompile` and `EffectComposer` do not work on either WebGPURenderer backend. Six files in this repo use them (about 26 occurrences), including `render/postProcessing.ts` and `render/haze.ts`.

**What WebGPU would buy:** better 4K upscaling and anti-aliasing (TAAU, which takes a 1080p-1440p image to 4K in one pass), plus motion blur from real motion vectors, ambient occlusion, reflections and screen-space GI. The WebGL add-ons have no motion vectors. Their TAA does not reproject, so it only works when nothing moves. Their ambient occlusion and reflection passes re-render the whole scene. Re-check at r187/r188: switch only if the split-screen bugs are fixed and a 4-viewport test on the M1 is no slower on CPU than WebGL.

**Browsers on macOS:** Chrome has had WebGPU since 113, Safari since 26 (September 2025), and Firefox since 145 on macOS 26 and 147 on every macOS version for Apple Silicon. Global support is about 87%. Public TV setups still need WebGL2, either the fallback or staying on WebGL.

**Budgets on the M1 (estimates):**
- **4K is out at native resolution.** The M1 GPU has about 2.6 TFLOPS and 68 GB/s shared memory, so 4K gets about a quarter of the per-pixel budget of 1080p. Render at 1080p (up to 1440p for one viewport) with dynamic resolution, then upscale. On WebGL, use browser scaling plus an FSR1-style sharpen in GLSL; on WebGPU, use TAAU.
- **Draw calls:** about 1,000 per frame for one viewport, 1,200 for two and 1,500 at most for four.
- **Shadows:** one shared sun shadow map in four-player mode.
- **Textures:** under 1-1.5 GB, all KTX2.
- **Post effects by preset:** about 6-8 for one player, about 5 for two, about 3-4 for four. Skip reflections and screen-space GI at two or more viewports; use baked lighting instead.

**Split-screen changes:**
- **Single post pass.** Total pixels stay the same with more viewports; what grows is draw submission, shadow renders and the fixed cost of each post-processing chain. Rendering every viewport into one shared HDR target and running one post chain should give the biggest saving on either renderer. It needs per-viewport edge clamping so bloom does not bleed across the split lines.
- **ArrayCamera on WebGPU.** WebGPU's `ArrayCamera` draws all viewports in one pass. Anything visible in any viewport is drawn in all of them, and nobody has shown it working with TAA.

**Draw-call reduction:**
- **BatchedMesh** is one call per batch on WebGL. On WebGPU it is a loop of cheap draws.
- **Indirect draws** and compute culling only work on the WebGPU backend.
- **Track layout:** split each track into roughly 100-200 m chunks with instancing for repeated props, LOD and frustum culling.
- **Shader precompile:** compile shaders on the loading screen so the race start does not hitch.

**Gaps:**
- I could not fetch the official three.js WebGPURenderer manual page, so its "experimental" wording comes from a second-hand guide.
- I found no confirmation that the June 2026 split-screen bug is fixed.
- Nobody has published a test of the CPU-cost gap on r184-r186.
- I could not confirm on Apple Silicon:
  - whether Safari 26 enables WebGPU on macOS Sonoma or Sequoia
  - `WEBGL_multi_draw` (what BatchedMesh's single-call path uses)
  - GPU timer queries for driving dynamic resolution
  - whether MSAA stays cheap on the M1's tile-based GPU through Chrome

Notes saved to `/home/user/game-gang/research_notes/Forza level browser racing game/car_rendering_cameras.md`. There is one section for each of the six key questions, each with Takeaway, Cited Findings, Inferences and Gaps. No talks from Turn 10, Polyphony, Playground or Codemasters were found, so all recommended starting values are marked as inferences to tune in-game.

Main findings:

- **Car paint:**
  - The official three.js baselines are:
    - Car example: metalness 1, roughness 0.5, clearcoat 1, clearcoatRoughness 0.03.
    - Clearcoat example's flake paint: metalness 0.9, roughness 0.5, clearcoatRoughness 0.1, `FlakesTexture` normal map with repeat 10×6 and normalScale 0.15.
  - `clearcoatNormalMap` gives the clear coat its own normals. That lets flakes sit under a smooth coat, with an optional orange-peel texture on top.
  - The installed three.js r186 includes `examples/jsm/tsl/WebGLNodesHandler.js`. With it, TSL `MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial` runs inside the existing `WebGLRenderer` (official example `webgl_tsl_clearcoat`). So a TSL flake and colour-shift paint is possible without moving to WebGPU. Check first that node materials pick up the project's ShaderChunk fog patches.
  - Unreal's car paint is a clear coat over a coloured base plus a flake ("glint") layer. Epic released a free pack of 280 automotive materials for UE 5.7 in March 2026.
  - The notes include presets for solid, metallic, pearlescent and matte paint. Don't use `sheen` for paint: three.js documents it as a cloth layer.
- **Glass:** a transparent car window (`transmission`) is very expensive in split screen. In r186 it re-renders every opaque object into an extra per-camera render target, sized to the viewport (checked in `WebGLRenderer.js`). Keep the current opaque dark glass, and use alpha blending for bumper or cockpit cams.
- **Reflections:**
  - Forza 7 used dynamic cube maps "to better seat the cars in the world"; Forza Motorsport (2023) uses ray tracing.
  - A dynamic cube costs 6 extra scene renders, which isn't affordable for 4 cars in 4 viewports.
  - Recommended layers:
    - Low preset: the existing sky reflection (HDRI PMREM) plus a fake asphalt lower half.
    - Default: reflection probes baked along the track spline at load time, which costs nothing per frame.
    - 1–2 players: one shared live reflection (`CubeCamera`) updating one face per frame.
  - r186 also adds `LightProbeGridWebGL` for baked, position-dependent diffuse light such as tunnels and tree shade.
- **Lights:** use emissive materials pushed into the existing HDR bloom, not real lights; the notes include an intensity ladder. Brake lights are a key readability cue in split screen. The stock `Lensflare` reads back the framebuffer, which likely fails with the MSAA HDR target (not tested); do flares in the composite shader instead. `SpotLight.map` is available for a headlight cookie on the player's own car at night.
- **Car models and licences:**
  - The free CC0 packs (Kenney, Quaternius, RG Poly, and the current Rgsdev car) are all stylised low-poly.
  - Sketchfab CC-BY models can be used commercially with credit. CC licences do not grant trademark rights, so real-car models (like the Ferrari and Porsche in the three.js demos) are out.
  - Fab's Standard License allows commercial use with no attribution. The Personal and Professional tiers give the same rights; the tier depends on the buyer's revenue ($100k).
  - Use the Speed Dreams models only for specs and dimensions; don't upgrade them.
  - The notes propose per-viewport LOD budgets (40–80k triangles down to under 1k) and a runtime livery built on a second UV set, kept under the clear coat. `DecalGeometry` distorts around corners.
- **Cameras:**
  - Criterion's GDC 2018 "Vehicle Feel Masterclass" covers camera movement, but it is members-only.
  - Eiserloh's GDC 2016 shake method: a 0–1 "trauma" value, shake scaled by trauma squared or cubed, driven by Perlin noise.
  - Allen Chou and Unreal show how to set up critically damped springs.
  - Measured browser chase-cam evidence: smoothing in world space leaves the camera 4–9 m behind where it should be at speed. Smoothing the offset in the car's own frame cut the hidden road ahead from 26.7 m to 10.7 m at 85 km/h.
  - The notes include a recommended rig: speed-scaled distance, height and FOV; look-ahead using the track spline; FOV handling for split screen; bumper, cockpit and TV/replay cams.

Gaps:
- No published polygon or texture budgets from racing studios.
- No verified free, realistic car of an original design; this needs a manual search on Sketchfab and Fab.
- The Fab licence terms for models shipped in a browser game weren't checked.
- The findings of the 2017 Holm et al. paper on perceived camera speed couldn't be retrieved.
- No measured M1 cost for cube cameras or the paint shaders.

I wrote the research notes for the track environment and lighting topic to `/home/user/game-gang/research_notes/Forza level browser racing game/track_environment_lighting.md`. There are eight sections, one per key question, each with a takeaway, cited findings, inferences and gaps. Pre-2024 sources are marked [older]. My frame-budget figures are estimates matched to the sibling note `rendering_platform_performance.md`, not measurements.

The request you sent with this run was "where can i see that something is running". This research task can't answer that, so the main session needs to.

Main findings:

- **r186 already has new tools for this, found by reading the installed three@0.186.1 package:**
  - `SunLight`/`SunLightShadow`: a sun light with 2 shadow cascades built into the WebGL shaders (1024² per cascade, 10% fade between them).
  - `LightProbeGridWebGL`/`LightProbeGrid`: a grid of light probes baked on the GPU, with bounces and a few probes per frame if wanted. It can be baked while the track loads instead of shipped.
  - `LoftGeometry`: builds a mesh from a series of cross-sections, which suits road, kerbs and barriers.
  - The WebGL `Sky` addon now has procedural clouds.
  - `PCFSoftShadowMap` is deprecated and falls back to `PCFShadowMap`.
  - `KTX2Loader` supports compressed HDR textures (BasisU UASTC HDR).
  - Materials have `alphaToCoverage` and `alphaHash`, for clean leaf edges with and without MSAA.
- **Split screen multiplies shadow cost.** The cascades are re-rendered for each viewport camera. The cheaper design:
  - Bake static track lighting in Blender into a second UV set, wired in code with `lightMap.channel = 1`.
  - Keep dynamic shadows for cars and nearby props only, within 150–250 m.
  - Put a blob AO patch under each car.
- **Vegetation:**
  - Use agargaro's MIT-licensed `InstancedMesh2` and `octahedral-impostor` libraries. Their demo shows 200k trees, with a simplified mesh at 15–100 units and impostors beyond that.
  - For grass, use instanced clump quads near the track only. A forum rule of thumb puts the total budget around 3M triangles.
  - The only M1 data point is a closed-source WebGPU grass system that holds 60 fps at 1440p.
- **Terrain:** four splat layers (8 texture fetches) plus a macro variation texture. Use triplanar only on steep faces, and hex tiling only on grass and gravel; combining it with triplanar raises the count to up to 27 fetches per map.
- **Sky and scenery:**
  - The r186 `Sky` addon with clouds plus sun-tinted height fog is enough to start.
  - The takram Bruneton atmosphere and cloud packages are beta and need a different post-processing library, so leave them for later.
  - Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data is free with attribution, but I couldn't confirm commercial-use terms from the excerpts. Read the full licence before relying on it.
- **Pipeline:** a hybrid with one source of truth.
  - A TypeScript trackgen turns the Speed Dreams XML into the centre line, the road and kerb meshes, the physics mesh, terrain and placement data.
  - Blender, run from the command line, adds landmarks and bakes lightmaps.
  - The road mesh is never edited by hand. The TORCS docs say doing so breaks alignment with physics.
- **Lighting presets:** start with fixed time-of-day presets (2–3 baked sets per track), and add a sun-independent AO bake later if a live day cycle is wanted.

**Gaps:**
- No studio publishes vegetation density or LOD distances for Forza, ACC or GT7, and the Digital Foundry Forza interview segments weren't available as text.
- I found no M1 timings for shadows, impostors or hex tiling. The shadow numbers come from integrated Intel GPUs.
- The exact Blender bake API arguments weren't checked against the official docs.
- There is no Speed Dreams data in the repo yet, so the XML element names are taken from the TORCS v4 manual and haven't been checked against real Speed Dreams files.

I've written the research notes on assets, the web pipeline, licensing and trademark risks. The file has the four required sections, and each has a takeaway, sourced findings, my own conclusions and open gaps. This is not legal advice, and several answers depend on jurisdiction.

**Assets**
- **Environment:** Poly Haven and ambientCG are both CC0, so they are free for commercial use with no credit needed. Counted on 2026-10-09:
  - Poly Haven: 521 models (about 110 nature, 37 rocks, 20 trees), 997 HDRIs and 867 textures.
  - ambientCG: 2,014 materials, including 78 asphalt and 51 road surfaces, plus 433 HDRIs.
- **Higher-quality paid option:** Fab/Megascans under Fab's Standard licence. Fab's summary says it can be used in any engine.
- **Free audio:** the cleanest sources are CC0 recordings on Freesound and the Sonniss GDC archive (royalty-free, no credit needed, but no AI training and no resale as standalone files).
- **Paid engine-sound packs:** the Magic Sound Effects packs have the RPM loops, but their listings say both "one commercial project" and "commercial purposes". Get written confirmation before buying.
- **Fonts:** OFL fonts are fine. Ship the licence text, and rename a font if you cut it down to fewer characters.

**Speed Dreams data**
- **Licence:** the Free Art License allows commercial use. Copies must carry the licence or a link to it, name the authors and say where the originals are. Anything derived from the data must stay under that licence or a compatible one, such as CC BY-SA 4.0.
- **Keeping our code separate:** if the derived track and car data ship as separate files, our code most likely stays outside that requirement. This is my reading of sections 3 and 4 of the licence; no official source settles it.
- **Code:** Speed Dreams code is GPL v2 or later. Porting its physics code to TypeScript would make our client code GPL too.
- **Sounds:** its credits file only covers sounds added in Nov 2024. Older samples such as `ferrarif355.wav`, `lamborghinidiablo.wav` and `mclarenf1.wav` have no stated source. Two sounds are labelled "CC-BY" but were taken from YouTube videos. Do not ship any Speed Dreams 1.4 sound; use the original CC0 Freesound recordings instead.
- **The one car still in the repo:** "sc-cavallo-360" is under the Free Art License, but its name suggests a Ferrari 360 lookalike.

**Trademark and IP risks**
- **Forza:** Microsoft registered FORZA for game software in Canada (December 2023). Keep "Forza" out of every public name, URL and ad.
- **Real circuits:** Laguna Seca actively licenses its name to Forza, Gran Turismo and iRacing (2026 press release). Rudskogen is in iRacing and runs 3.254 km with 14 turns, so the 3.3 km club circuit shouldn't copy it. Use invented names and original layouts.
- **Real car shapes:** the Humvee ruling in Call of Duty (2020) protected realistic depictions, but the 2023 Jack Daniel's ruling narrowed that defence. Both are US-only, and EU registered designs protect car shapes (Ferrari's GTA IV claim relied on them). Use made-up makes with blended silhouettes, and strip logos from downloaded models.

**Pipeline and hosting**
- **Compression:** use meshopt for geometry, which is the gltf-transform 4.5.1 default and decodes faster than Draco. Use KTX2 textures: ETC1S for colour maps, UASTC with zstd 18–19 for normal and ORM maps.
- **Settings for cars:** turn off flattening, joining and simplification so wheels stay separate objects.
- **Texture memory:** by my calculation, about 40 2k textures drop from roughly 850 MB to 210 MB of GPU memory.
- **Download targets:** about 15–20 MB to reach the lobby, about 30–60 MB per track streamed during the lobby, about 250 MB total. These are my design suggestions, based on CrazyGames' 50 / 20 / 250 MB limits.
- **Caching:** hashed file names cached for a year as immutable, the HTML page always revalidated, and a service worker for repeat visits.
- **Hosting:**
  - Vercel's Hobby plan is non-commercial only, so a subscription product needs Pro ($20/month, 1 TB included, then $0.15–$0.35/GB).
  - Cloudflare R2 has free egress, and its terms allow large files hosted on R2.
  - At an assumed 15 TB a month (about 100k monthly users), that is roughly $2,100–$4,900/month on Vercel against a few dollars on R2. Keep the app on Vercel Pro and serve game assets from R2.

**Open gaps**
- The per-folder licences in the 1.4 data are unchecked.
- I found no free, realistic, original-design car.
- The US owner of FORZA and whether Laguna Seca or Rudskogen are registered marks are unknown.
- UAE law isn't covered.
- The three.js r186 loader setup and which compressed texture formats Chrome on an M1 supports are unconfirmed.

Main findings:

**Best-looking web racers today (2025-2026)**
- **Visual high end:** custom three.js projects on WebGPU with TSL shaders.
  - Bruno Simon's 2025 portfolio (Awwwards case study, March 2026).
  - "threejspunk" by Anderson Mancini (three.js forum, September 2026): rain, reflections, 50+ missions, multiplayer.
- **Unity:** Unity 6 WebGPU is now a real option. Ashline Racing shipped on it in June 2025, and Unity 6.6 (September 2026) made WebGPU production-supported, though not the default. The 6.6 details come from a secondary news site.
- **Most-played web racers:** Madalin Stunt Cars 2 and Drift Hunters (both Unity WebGL) and PolyTrack (three.js + Ammo.js) succeed on instant play and handling, not looks.
- **PlayCanvas, Babylon.js, Needle, Godot:** none of them turned up a racing showcase that sets a visual bar.

**Techniques**
- **Slow Roads** (2023, older but the most detailed write-up found):
  - Full detail only in a narrow corridor beside the road.
  - Scenery chunks are generated gradually, ahead of need.
  - Memory and buffers are reused to avoid pauses.
  - Collisions are a simple distance check to the road centre.
  - Converting images to WebP halved the bundle.
  - Over 97% of players load in under 10 seconds.
  - Only 52% of players get above 55 FPS. That is the strongest evidence that automatic quality presets matter.
- **Bruno Simon:**
  - The world is authored in Blender, where object names drive physics and game data.
  - Textures are compressed GPU formats (ETC1S/UASTC) and models are Draco-compressed.
  - Grass is about 78,400 single-triangle blades merged into one geometry.
  - Repeated objects are instanced.
  - The mobile preset turns off water blur and depth of field and lowers shadow quality.

**Business models**
- **AirConsole Hero pricing:** sources conflict. The App Store snapshot (July 2026) shows $7.99 monthly and $29.99 lifetime, plus unlabelled tiers from $2.99 to $23.99. Older figures were $4.99/month or $23.99/year (about 2020) and $3.99/month (2018).
- **AirConsole model:**
  - The free tier is a weekly selection of games, 2 players maximum, with ad breaks. The breaks advertise Hero itself, not third parties.
  - One Hero subscriber in a session unlocks extra content for everyone.
  - Paid perks may never give a gameplay advantage.
  - Developers are paid from subscription revenue, split by the games each subscriber played. Subscribers spend about half their playtime in one favourite game.
  - AirConsole is also moving into cars: BMW, and VW tied to a $149/year in-vehicle plan.
- **Jackbox:**
  - Sells annual five-game packs; Party Pack 11 was $29.99.
  - Reports players joining its games 826 million times since December 2022.
  - Now offers a game collection on Netflix.
  - Is building a free, ad-supported smart-TV streaming service due by the end of 2026.

**What makes a party platform "worth it"**
- The most detailed review I found is from 2018 (CGMagazine, 7/10). It faulted:
  - a weak long tail of games;
  - touch controls for free-movement games;
  - lag.

  It also said no single game justified the price.
- For Split Ways, that makes touch steering and controller latency product-critical.
- It also argues for a standout flagship plus a steady stream of new content, not a large but shallow catalogue.

**Gaps:**
- No published frame rates on Apple Silicon or download sizes for any of these games.
- No confirmed current AirConsole price, revenue-share percentage, or 2024-2026 value review.
- No Jackbox revenue or Netflix deal terms.

I saved the notes to `/home/user/game-gang/research_notes/Forza level browser racing game/handling_feel_audio.md`. They cover all six key questions in the three-part structure from researcher.md, with sources inline and older material marked by year.

The main findings:

1. **Speed Dreams has moved on.** Its main branch (on forge.a-lec.org, updated 2026-10-07) now contains only `simuv5`; simuv2, 2.1, 3 and 4 are gone. It still reads the same car XML names, so Speed Dreams 1.4 specs remain usable. I read the current source directly; the original TORCS simuv2 source could not be fetched, so "same formulas" is an inference from shared lineage.
2. **What the tyre parameters mean** (from simuv5 `wheel.cpp`):
   - The shape factor is C = 2 − asin(RFactor)·2/π, so "dynamic friction %" is the grip left in a full slide, as a fraction of peak.
   - "stiffness" (Ca) sets the initial slope of the curve, B = Ca/C, and E is the "elasticity factor".
   - Grip falls off with load: mu × (lfMin + (lfMax − lfMin)·exp(lfK·Fz/opLoad)). At the "operating load" the factor is exactly 1.
   - Braking and cornering slip are combined into one vector (sx, sin α), which gives a friction circle.
   - The simulation runs at 500 Hz (`RCM_MAX_DT_SIMU` = 0.002 s).
   - The notes also give the formulas for engine torque and engine braking, gearbox inertia and shift time, the seven differential types, and aero drag (0.645·Cx·A) with ground effect.
3. **Worked example (sc-cavallo-360, the one car left in the Speed Dreams data repo):** C = 1.772, B = 12.41, E = 0.86. Grip peaks at about 0.16 combined slip (roughly 9° slip angle). Gear top speeds at the 8500 rpm limiter are 69 / 116 / 155 / 197 / 243 / 294 km/h, and drag is about 2.8 kN at 300 km/h.
4. **Rapier's vehicle controller is the root of the arcade feel.** Rapier 0.21.0 was published 2026-09-25 and its controller is a port of Bullet's raycast vehicle. It does not simulate wheel spin, slip ratio, a tyre curve, engine, gearbox, differential or aero. Sideways grip is a constraint that cancels sliding until it hits a cap (suspension force × dt × frictionSlip, default 10.5), so cars grip fully and then suddenly slide.
5. **Recommended handling setup:**
   - Keep Rapier for the car body, collisions and optionally the suspension raycasts.
   - Setting `frictionSlip` to 0 should switch off the controller's own friction; this is read from the source and not yet tested.
   - Apply a custom tyre model with `addForceAtPoint`.
   - Run Rapier at a fixed 120 Hz with 2–4 tyre/wheel substeps per step (240–480 Hz).
6. **Assists:** the notes give concrete algorithms and starting values for ABS and traction control (hold wheel slip at the curve's peak), stability control, steering assist that caps steering angle by speed, counter-steer assist, braking assist and a racing-line overlay. They also cover touch steering (dead zone, response curve, speed-sensitive lock, a steering-rate limit) and an explicit D/N/R reverse with a clear "R" on the HUD. These touch and assist numbers are my design recommendations, not sourced values.
7. **Engine sound:** the industry baseline is still crossfaded RPM loops split into on-load and off-load layers; granular tools (REV, AudioMotors) are the upgrade. The notes include a Web Audio design and a browser procedural example (SpudzzDev/en). For sourcing:
   - Freesound CC0 and CC-BY sounds are fine commercially; the non-commercial ones are not.
   - Sonniss GDC bundles are royalty-free.
   - Magic Sound Effects Car Engines Vol. 2 ($30, 80 RPM loops) has contradictory licence text, so confirm in writing before buying.
8. **Gaps:**
   - No official Forza 2023 description of how its assists work.
   - No primary source on touch-steering filtering in mobile racers.
   - No 2024–2026 source on browser granular engine audio; the best sources are from 2013–2014.
   - Nothing on phone recording technique or the legality of recording your own car.
   - The HUD sources are tool changelogs and forums, not UX research.

I saved the report to `/home/user/game-gang/reports/Forza level browser racing game.md`: 8,352 words with 120 inline source citations, covering every area you asked for and ending with milestones M8 to M15+. All the owner decisions are applied, and research suggestions that went against them were dropped.

**Main conclusions:**
- **Rendering:** a locked 60 fps on the M1 Air driving a 4K TV works only if the game renders at about 1080p internally and upscales. It should stay on three.js WebGLRenderer r186 for now. WebGPU costs about twice the CPU per draw and still has split-screen bugs. Most lighting should be baked, all viewports should share one post-processing chain, and quality presets should switch automatically based on GPU time. 1080p and 4K TVs can use the same budget. None of these budgets has been measured on an M1, so the first milestone has to profile on the real device.
- **Handling:** Rapier's built-in vehicle controller is why the car feels "on rails, then sliding". The current build works around it with gravity set to 13 and grip/yaw assists. The fix is a per-wheel tyre model built from Speed Dreams' published formulas and car specs, with physics at 120 Hz plus substeps. Assists should be on by default, with Assisted, Pro and Sim presets per player.
- **Controller:** a floating, horizontal-only drag steer replaces tilt, with "Buttons" kept as the simple option. Reverse stays "hold brake" but becomes impossible to miss. The item button is gone. Haptics only work on Android, so on-screen visual feedback is the main channel on every phone.
- **Assets and legal:**
  - CC0 sources (Poly Haven, ambientCG) cover the environment.
  - The weak spot is cars. No free, realistic, original-design car model was found, so the free models will need in-house rework.
  - Never port Speed Dreams code (GPL) or ship its sounds.
  - Track and car data derived from Speed Dreams must ship as separate files under its share-alike licence.
  - Never use "Forza" or real circuit and car names publicly, and run a name clearance search before launch.
- **Business:** the host pays and one subscription unlocks the room. Subscribers on similar platforms spend about half their time in one favourite game, so one excellent racer with a monthly content drop matters more than a big catalogue. I suggest about $6.99/month, tested against $7.99, with a 3–4-week trial. Keep the app on Vercel Pro (Hobby is non-commercial) and serve assets from Cloudflare R2 to avoid large bandwidth bills.
- **UI:** the current TV UI has the generic "AI-generated" look (gradient glows, frosted glass panels, one techno font) and text far too small for a TV. The report recommends a race-weekend broadcast look built from in-engine renders, with strict text-size and screen-edge rules for TV.

**Build order:**
- M8: Track 1, a 3.3 km club circuit, plus the track generator, profiling and presets.
- M9: handling, assists, the new controller, HUD and engine audio.
- M10: cars and cameras.
- M11: Track 2, a 5.9 km fast autodrome, with vegetation and the lighting bake.
- M12: Track 3, a 3.8 km mountain road.
- M13: the premium TV and website UI.
- M14: subscription and launch.
- M15+: a new track or car pack every month.

M8 also retires the existing items mode (mystery boxes, drift boost, boost pads) and the Corniche Run track. Slipstream stays as physics.

issues.problem: The plan does not start with the first three tracks. Track 1 is M8, then Feel (M9) and Cars and cameras (M10) come before Track 2 (M11) and Track 3 (M12). The claim that each track milestone adds one major system is also false: M8 covers cleanup, profiling, a render-path rewrite, trackgen v1, Track 1 and the controller replacement. The track notes' order of work (generator plus club circuit, then vegetation and impostors, then the bake, then the 5.9 km track, then the mountain road) has no feel or car milestones in between. Separately, no gate tests the 2-player Medium preset until M12.
issues.fix: Make M8-M10 Tracks 1-3, each with one system: Track 1 = trackgen, performance foundation and the minimum touch controller; Track 2 = vegetation and the Blender bake; Track 3 = elevation terrain. Then run Feel, Cars, UI and Subscription. If feel must come earlier on purpose, fold it into the track milestones, or rewrite the heading and summary to match the real order. Add a 2-player Medium 60 fps check to the M8 gate.

issues.where: Conclusion, para 2: 'Touch-only control... is the product's main point of difference against free TV party games'
issues.problem: The notes treat touch control as the main risk: free-movement games on touch are where reviewers said platforms fail. They name visual quality at a locked 60 fps, plus depth and variety, as the point of difference (state_of_the_art §5). The report's own 'Where Split Ways can stand out' bullet says the same. The conclusion reverses this.
issues.fix: Say that touch control is the biggest product risk and must be the best-tested part of the game. Say the point of difference is premium visuals at a locked 60 fps in 4-player split screen, plus monthly content depth.

issues.where: Conclusion: 'Rendering on an M1 at 4K is a solved budgeting exercise'; summary: 'achievable... at a locked 60 fps'; tyre section: 'Four cars × four wheels × 480 Hz is trivial work for V8'
issues.problem: The notes say every budget is an unmeasured estimate. There are no three.js per-pass timings on an M1, the shadow costs come from Intel integrated GPUs, and neither the tyre loop nor Rapier at 120 Hz has been benchmarked. The report's own Gap line says the same, so the conclusion contradicts it.
issues.fix: Call it a budget plan that M8 profiling must prove. Mark the tyre and physics cost as an estimate to measure.

issues.where: Assists section (Assisted/Pro/Sim presets) vs Steering section (Off/Assist/Autopilot); M9 'Done when: Assisted lap times are slower than Sim'
issues.problem: The report defines two separate per-player assist systems, both picked in the lobby, and never reconciles them. The handicap evidence in the notes (Asphalt TouchDrive players are slower) is about steering autopilot, not ABS, TC or stability control. On a real tyre model those assists usually make novices faster, so this gate could fail by design.
issues.fix: Merge the two into one assist ladder (for example Autopilot > Assisted > Pro > Sim) with a clear mapping. Tie the handicap gate to Autopilot/Assist vs Off, not to ABS/TC vs Sim.

issues.where: M8 'Clean up for the owner's decisions': 'Retire items mode... along with its arcade speed tricks (drift boost, boost pads)'
issues.problem: The owner only banned Mario Kart items. No note recommends removing drift boost or boost pads, yet the report lists this as an owner decision.
issues.fix: Keep items removal as the owner decision. List removing drift boost and boost pads as a separate sim-lite recommendation that needs owner approval.

issues.where: Why not WebGPU yet: 'Six Split Ways files (about 26 call sites) would need a TSL rewrite'
issues.problem: Two of the six files belong to features M8 removes under owner decisions: scene/itemVisuals.ts (items, 4 matches) and scene/sea.ts (the Corniche coastal sea, 1 match). After cleanup the port covers 4 files and about 21 call sites.
issues.fix: State the post-M8 scope: postProcessing.ts, haze.ts, particles.ts and sceneryModels.ts, about 21 call sites.

issues.where: Engine sound 'Per car: 6-10 on-load and 6-10 off-load loops'; M9 'Engine audio v1: ...three engine types, cut from CC0 recordings'
issues.problem: The assets notes say the CC0 recordings Speed Dreams credits are fly-bys and revs, not steady-RPM holds, and that no free source has on-load/off-load layers. The realistic free route gives about 4-6 RPM layers. Neither 'three engine types' nor 12-20 loops per car from fly-bys is supported.
issues.fix: Set v1 at 4-6 RPM layers cut from steady segments of CC0 recordings. Add a sourcing step (written licence confirmation for a paid pack, or our own recordings) before promising full on/off-load sets.

issues.where: Speed Dreams section ('Free Art License 1.3 allows commercial use'); M8 'Derived track data is shipped under FAL'
issues.problem: The notes flag that the per-directory licences in the 1.4 tarball are unverified for the 29 track layouts and the car setups. Some data may be GPL 'functional data', and it is unknown whether SD tracks copy real circuits. The report treats all 1.4 data as FAL.
issues.fix: Add an M8 task: check the licence file of each SD 1.4 track or car before deriving from it, and record it in the licence log.

issues.where: M12 Terrain: 'Copernicus GLO-30, which requires its prescribed credit'
issues.problem: The notes say the licence excerpts seen did not include an explicit commercial-use clause and the full licence must be read. The report presents attribution as the only condition.
issues.fix: Mark commercial use of GLO-30 in a subscription product as unverified until the full licence is read. Keep synthetic erosion terrain as the fallback.

issues.where: M10 Car line-up: '6-8 cars... built from free CC0 or CC-BY models of original designs'
issues.problem: The notes suggest 4-6 base bodies, not 6-8. The research also found no usable free, realistic, original-design car, and says a manual Sketchfab search with licence checks is needed. M10 assumes those models exist and has no step to find them.
issues.fix: Add a car-sourcing step before M10 (candidate list, licence check, real-silhouette check). Plan 4-6 base bodies with variants, or explain how 6-8 cars will be reached.

issues.where: Reflections layers (Low = HDRI only; 'Medium (the default)') vs Automatic quality presets table (Low = 'baked probes')
issues.problem: The two sections disagree on what Low includes. The reflections section calls Medium 'the default', while the preset table picks the preset by player count. It is unclear what to build for each preset.
issues.fix: Use one definition. Either Low uses baked probes and the reflections section drops 'HDRI only', or the preset table drops probes from Low. Remove 'the default' or tie it to player count.

issues.where: Feedback, iPhone: 'Wake Lock works from iOS 16.4' (next to the Add to Home Screen recommendation)
issues.problem: The notes say that in home-screen web apps, Wake Lock only works from about iOS 18.4. iOS 16.4-18.4 failed in standalone mode, and the lock must be re-acquired after the page is hidden. The report recommends home-screen mode without this caveat.
issues.fix: Say Wake Lock works in Safari from 16.4 but in home-screen web apps only from about 18.4. Keep the re-request and the 'Tap to resume' fallback.

issues.where: TV UI '10-foot basics' and the M13 'Done when' list
issues.problem: Focus states are missing. The TV notes stress an unmistakable focus state visible from the couch: about 1.05-1.1 scale, a brand-colour outline, Apple-style spacing so focused items don't overlap, and showing which player has control. Neither the basics list nor the M13 gate mentions it.
issues.fix: Add a focus-state rule to the 10-foot basics and a focus check to the M13 gate.

issues.where: Summary: 'Touch controls are where reviewers have criticised phone-controller platforms most'
issues.problem: The source is one 2018 CGMagazine review that also criticised clones and lag, and the notes flag it as dated. 'Reviewers... most' overstates it.
issues.fix: Say: 'The main (2018) AirConsole Hero review criticised frustrating free-movement touch games, along with clones and lag.'

issues.where: Price bullet: 'Benchmarks are... AirConsole Hero at $7.99'
issues.problem: The notes say AirConsole Hero pricing sources conflict ($3.99 / $4.99 / $7.99) and the current official price is unconfirmed. The pricing bullet uses $7.99 as a firm benchmark.
issues.fix: Qualify it as '$7.99 in a July 2026 App Store snapshot; official price unconfirmed'.
